implementation_notes: Camel implements the pattern as a step inside a route: resequence(expression) orders messages by an expression such as a sequence header, in either batch mode (collect up to size messages or timeout, sort, then send - the default, 100 messages or 1 s) or stream mode (gap detection: emit as soon as the next expected number arrives, with capacity bounding the backlog, timeout advancing past a hole, and rejectOld raising MessageRejectedException for anything older than the last delivered message). Duplicates collapse to the last message unless allowDuplicates is enabled, and ignoreInvalidExchanges keeps unparseable messages out of the resequencer. The sibling variant (spring-integration-resequencer) instead models the problem as message groups over a MessageGroupStore, which trades the in-route buffer for durable group state, release strategies and a discard channel.
pitfalls: Camel's stream mode advances the expected sequence number on timeout precisely so the route is not blocked; without rejectOld, a message that arrives after that skip is simply delivered late and the stream is out of order again.
The defaults (capacity 1000, batch 100 messages / 1 s) silently decide the behaviour of a route: a burst above capacity or a gap longer than the timeout changes which messages come out in order.
Batch mode sorts by the expression and needs either a size bound or a timeout to fire; relying on the batch size alone stalls when the producer emits fewer messages than the bound.

variants.name: Spring Integration <resequencer> over a MessageGroupStore
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Integration treats the resequencer as an aggregator that does not modify messages: messages are correlated (CORRELATION_ID by default), buffered in a MessageGroupStore and released in SEQUENCE_NUMBER order. release-partial-sequences decides whether contiguous runs go out as soon as they are available or the whole group must arrive, a release strategy can replace the SEQUENCE_SIZE default, and group-timeout with send-partial-result-on-expiry - or a discard-channel - defines what happens when the missing message never arrives; expire-group-upon-timeout drops late arrivals instead of letting them start a group that can never complete. The configuration is declarative, so the policy is reviewable as configuration rather than buried in consumer code.
variants.code_sketch:
<int:channel id="scrambled"/>
<int:channel id="ordered"/>
<int:resequencer input-channel="scrambled" output-channel="ordered"
  correlation-strategy-expression="headers['orderId']"
  release-strategy-expression="size() == 10"
  release-partial-sequences="true"
  group-timeout="4000" send-partial-result-on-expiry="true"
  discard-channel="lateMessages"/>
<int:channel id="lateMessages"/>   <!-- what the gap policy dropped -->
pitfalls: The default in-memory MessageGroupStore loses every pending group on restart; a persistent store is required when ordering must survive a restart, and a message-store reaper is then needed to expire partial groups.
Spring Integration's own documentation warns that resequencing suits relatively short sequences with small gaps: many disjoint sequences with big gaps cost store and scheduler work per group.
release-partial-sequences=false without a sequence size means nothing is released until the group times out, which turns the resequencer into a latency source.
